target_customer: At launch, English speakers learning Chinese; later, language teachers and schools creating online speaking assignments
problem: Learners were tied to one textbook's vocabulary and had little engaging, customizable practice; later, teachers had few tools to assign and assess spoken work online.
business_model: Freemium web app (consumer games), later teacher subscriptions with free and paid plans
product_category: Language learning games, later classroom speaking assessment software

founders.name: Justin Cannon
founders.background_notes: Listed as founder on the YC page. A search snippet from a Boston Phoenix article ties him to MIT grads and an MIT Chinese course; that article was not opened, so education is left empty.

founders.name: Chris Varenhorst
founders.background_notes: Named by The Next Web (Dec 31, 2010) as a founder; not on the YC page.

exit.reason: Price undisclosed; the existing Lingt game product was to close on 2011-02-28 and live on inside Dictionary.com flashcards

competitors.name: Grockit
competitors.what: Social learning and test prep service, described as a TC50 alum

technical_complexity.rationale: Vocabulary matching games with dictionary-driven language support and speech input were standard web development; adding a language required only a new dictionary per TechCrunch.

defensibility.rationale: Vocabulary games were easy to copy and competitors such as Quizlet and Smart.fm already existed; the company was acquired about a year after launch.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Dictionary.com acquired the game service on 2010-12-31 and folded it into its flashcards product.

market_need_then: Learners wanted customizable vocabulary practice beyond one textbook; TechCrunch noted vocabulary only content at launch in December 2009, and no demand figures were found.

branding.domain_note: Uses lingt.com; earlier lingtlanguage.com per a Boston Phoenix snippet.

rebrands.why: Not stated; a commenter and search snippets suggest the name was later shortened, unverified

branding.community_and_virality: Used in university courses such as an MIT OpenCourseWare Chinese course per a search snippet; site claims 10,000+ schools.

brand_strength.rationale: Niche recognition among language teachers; the invented name is easy to mistype and no sourced press on the brand.

pivots.from: Consumer language learning games for Chinese
pivots.to: Online speaking assignments and assessments for teachers
pivots.why: Not stated in opened sources; the date is unclear because listings give 2012 as the launch year of the teacher product

outcome_analysis: Lingt launched a Chinese vocabulary game in December 2009 after YC Summer 2009 and was acquired by Dictionary.com on December 31, 2010, with the game product closing in February 2011. A company called Lingt Language, Inc. now sells a teacher speaking assignment tool claiming 10,000 schools, so the original game exit and the current active business are linked by name and founder listing but the relationship is not documented in the sources opened.
notes: Status conflict: the YC directory says Active, while TNW reports Dictionary.com acquired the game service on 2010-12-31. The current lingt.com (Lingt Language, Inc., copyright 2026) sells a teacher tool; whether it is the same entity or a continuation after the acquisition is not established, and listings give 2012 as its launch year. The $20K YC funding rests on CB Insights alone. A Spanish startup database lists $10K and $125K seed entries without dates or investors and may refer to the teacher product; not recorded. Acquisition terms are undisclosed so failure factors are left empty. Competitor names come from TechCrunch Dec 20, 2009.
